source.author: cic
source.text: Itaque unum illud erat insitum priscis illis, quos cascos appellat Ennius, esse in morte sensum neque excessu vitae sic deleri hominem, ut funditus interiret; idque cum multis aliis rebus, tum e pontificio iure et e caerimoniis sepulcrorum intellegi licet, quas maxumis ingeniis praediti nec tanta cura coluissent nec violatas tam inexpiabili religione sanxissent, nisi haereret in eorum mentibus mortem non interitum esse omnia tollentem atque delentem, sed quandam quasi migrationem commutationemque vitae, quae in claris viris et feminis dux in caelum soleret esse, in ceteris humi retineretur et permaneret tamen.
source.text_original: Itaque unum illud erat insitum priscis illis, quos cascos appellat Ennius, esse in morte sensum neque excessu vitae sic deleri hominem, ut funditus interiret; / idque cum multis aliis rebus, tum e pontificio iure et e caerimoniis sepulcrorum intellegi licet, quas maxumis ingeniis praediti nec tanta cura coluissent nec violatas tam inexpiabili religione sanxissent, nisi haereret in eorum mentibus mortem non interitum esse omnia tollentem atque delentem, sed quandam quasi migrationem commutationemque vitae, quae in claris viris et feminis dux in caelum soleret esse, in ceteris humi retineretur et permaneret tamen.
source.text_english: Accordingly, this one belief was ingrained in those ancient men, whom Ennius calls casci: that there is perception in death, and that by the departure of life a human being is not so destroyed as to perish utterly. This may be understood from many other things, and especially from the pontifical law and the rites of burials, rites which men of the greatest genius would neither have observed with such care nor, if violated, have established with such inviolable religious sanction, unless it were fixed in their minds that death is not annihilation, which takes everything away and wipes everything out, but rather a kind of migration and change of life, which in distinguished men and women used to be a guide to heaven, while in the rest it remained and continued on earth.

reuse.text: nam et rudes illi Italiae homines, quos cascos Ennius appellat, qui sibi, ut in Rhetoricis Cicero ait, uictu fero uitam requirebant, ante chartae et membranarum usum aut in dedolatis ex ligno codicellis aut in corticibus arborum mutua epistularum alloquia missitabant; unde et portitores earum tabellarios et scriptores a libris arborum librarios uocauere.

reuse.text_english: For even those uncultivated men of Italy, whom Ennius calls casci, who, as Cicero says in the Rhetorica, sought out life for themselves by a savage means of living, before the use of paper and parchment used to send mutual messages in letters either on little tablets of wood smoothed down or on the bark of trees; whence they also called the bearers of these messages tabellarii, and the writers librarii, from the books of trees.
